column1: # WHAT THIS IS FOR, AND WHAT IT IS NOT FOR.
# These terms select which reviews go into the LABELLING POOL. They are a
# net for finding candidate examples of rare categories, nothing more.
# They are NOT a classifier and must never be reported as one. Rows found
# by these seeds carry stratum=seed_hit, and any recall number measured on
# them is circular by construction: the seeds found them, so of course the
# seeds match them. Recall is reported on the stratum=random_all rows only.
# See research/RISK_SCORING_MODEL_PLAN.md and the sampling note in the
# Sources: the vocabulary lists in research/HAZARD_SENTENCE_TAGGING_GUIDE.md
# section 2, which were themselves read off real reviews in this project's
# own scrapes; plus the safety regex already used in
#   subtype:  for safety only, a hazard_taxonomy subtype; "-" otherwise
#   BLOCK rows are false friends. Any BLOCK phrase found in a review is
#   masked out BEFORE seed matching, so "not legit dual shock 4" does not
#   count as a shock hazard. Section 6 of the tagging guide lists these.
# Matching is done on the normalized text (text_norm.normalize_text) with
# word boundaries, so "init" does not fire inside "initial".
# NOT "nagshort" or "nag-short": the normalizer strips the affix and leaves
# the bare word "short", which then fires on "short na damit", "short delay"
# and "short battery life". It produced 37 matches, nearly all junk. Reviews
# that really describe a short usually also say sunog/usok/spark, so they are
# still caught. Keep the unambiguous forms only.
# The normalizer strips affixes but keeps the particle "na", so "hindi na
# nag-charge" does not match the seed "hindi nag-charge". These variants
# exist because of that, not because they are different complaints.
# Found by reading the first generated queue. "kuryente" on its own means
# mains electricity far more often than an electric shock, and the pool
# carries clothing as well as electronics, where "mainit" is a complaint
# about a fabric and not a hazard.
